Chapter 2: The Challenge of Literal Obedience in Modern Life
As the days turned into weeks, this experiment started to settle into its own rhythm. Each month brought a different focus—modesty, domesticity, submission, motherhood, and more. The idea was simple: fully dive into each theme, and see what happens when ancient instructions run headfirst into the realities of a modern home.
The first real test? Modesty. You know those verses about clothing and appearance that get quoted a lot, but almost never followed to the letter? Well, for this experiment, it meant long skirts, covered arms, and a headscarf during prayer. Even a simple trip to the grocery store turned into an exercise in self-consciousness. Strangers stared, friends had questions, and the experimenter ended up feeling both exposed and invisible—all at the same time.
It was surprising how quickly clothes could shift the way someone feels. Suddenly, there was this new awareness of just how much attention we give to appearance, and how much of that comes from the world around us—not from scripture. Most of us don’t even realize how our idea of “appropriate” dress is handed down by culture, not by any sacred text.
But the challenge didn’t end with clothing. The Bible’s advice about women’s speech—especially the call to be “quiet” and “submissive”—was even tougher. In every conversation, whether with friends, at work, or at home, there was a constant tug-of-war: the urge to speak up versus the pressure to hold back. Pretty soon, it became clear—forced silence can feel a lot like being erased.
But here’s the twist: in those moments of listening, there was a new appreciation for the power of words, and how valuable restraint can be.
One afternoon, while folding laundry and thinking about the day’s efforts, the experimenter realized that “biblical womanhood” is really shaped by interpretation. The same passage that one person uses to demand silence can be read by someone else as a call to wisdom and discernment. It often comes down to which voices get heard—and which ones don’t.
There were also some unexpectedly beautiful moments. Trying to care for the poor and welcome strangers—another biblical command—opened up chances to reach out to neighbors, volunteer at shelters, and share meals with people in need. These acts didn’t feel like a burden at all. Instead, they offered glimpses of something sacred. You could feel that some instructions, when lived out, actually bring life and joy—while others can feel stifling or even harmful.
The hardest moments, though, came when the experiment clashed with deeply held values. The instruction to “submit” to a husband in all things was especially tough. There was one memorable day where the experimenter tried to let her husband make every decision—what to eat, where to go, how to spend money. The result? Frustration, on both sides. It became obvious: real partnership is built on mutual respect, not blind obedience.
Through all these months, the experimenter kept coming back to the same question—what does it really mean to be faithful? Is it about following rules? Or is it about seeking wisdom? There was never an easy answer. But the process brought a new sense of humility, and a realization that most of us are just doing our best to make sense of ancient words in a world that’s completely different from the one they were written for.
By the end of this phase, the experimenter had learned something important: to hold the Bible with both reverence and curiosity. It was no longer just a list of rules to follow, but more like a conversation partner—sometimes comforting, sometimes challenging, always complex.
